qs.e: Autism spectrum disorder is characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction alongside restricted, repetitive behaviors.

qs.q: A pediatrician evaluates an infant during a routine 12-month well-child visit for early behavioral signs of autism spectrum disorder. Which finding represents the earliest recognizable red flag?
o: Loss of spoken words at age three
Lack of peer interactive play skills
Failure to respond to own name
qs.e: Failure to respond to one's name by 12 months is one of the earliest social-communication red flags for autism. The other listed features typically become apparent much later in toddlerhood or childhood.

exam: What are the two core DSM‑5 domains for diagnosing ASD? — Social communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviours; both must be present in early development.

A 3‑year‑old has no eye contact, no words, and lines up toys. Which assessment tool would you choose in a low‑resource setting and why? — ADOS‑2 or ADI‑R; they provide structured observation when specialist input is limited.

How would you differentiate ASD from childhood‑onset schizophrenia in a 10‑year‑old? — Schizophrenia presents with hallucinations/delusions; ASD lacks psychotic symptoms and shows lifelong pattern of social deficits.
What is the first pharmacologic step for severe irritability in ASD and why avoid benzodiazepines? — Low‑dose risperidone; benzodiazepines can worsen cognition and cause dependence.
A child with ASD develops new seizures. What is your immediate management priority? — Obtain EEG if possible, start antiepileptic therapy, and assess for underlying metabolic causes.
Explain how maternal malaria in pregnancy could increase ASD risk. — Placental inflammation and hypoxia may disrupt fetal brain development, a recognised environmental risk factor.

When is genetic testing indicated in ASD and what result would change management? — When dysmorphic features or family history suggest a syndrome; identification of a treatable metabolic disorder (e.g., phenylketonuria) would alter therapy.

Describe one community‑based intervention feasible in East Africa for children with ASD. — Parent‑mediated ABA using locally available toys and visual schedules; improves communication without costly equipment.
ai.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with early‑onset deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviours. Diagnosis relies on developmental history and standardized criteria; severity guides support needs.

b: Use DSM‑5 or ICD‑11 criteria: (a) social‑communication deficits, (b) restricted/repetitive behaviours, both present in the developmental period.
Symptoms must cause clinically significant impairment and not be better explained by intellectual disability alone.
sections.p: Autism Spectrum Disorder is defined by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, plus restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, present from early childhood.

t.b: Confirms age of onset and pattern of deficits; distinguishes ASD from acquired conditions.
Provide structured observation and caregiver interview; essential where informal assessment is limited.

b: Level 1 – requires support; mild language delay, occasional social difficulty.
Level 2 – substantial support; marked language deficits, frequent repetitive behaviours.
Level 3 – very substantial support; minimal spoken language, severe behavioural rigidity.
sections.p: Severity is graded by level of support needed (DSM‑5 Level 1‑3) and by functional domains (communication, social interaction, behaviour).

b: Chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., 22q11.2 deletion).
Rare single‑gene disorders (e.g., Fragile X, Tuberous Sclerosis).
Maternal infections (e.g., rubella, malaria) and malnutrition.
Perinatal hypoxia, pre‑term birth.
sections.p: ASD is multifactorial: genetic predisposition, prenatal exposures, and perinatal complications. In low‑resource settings, consider co‑existing infections and nutritional factors.

b: No response to name by 12 months.
No babbling or gestures by 12 months; no words by 16 months.
Hand‑flapping, lining up toys, intense focus on parts of objects.
sections.p: Typical early signs appear before 2 years: poor eye contact, lack of joint attention, delayed babbling, and absent pointing. Later, repetitive motor stereotypies and insistence on sameness dominate.
Investigations aim to identify treatable comorbidities and underlying aetiologies; many are optional in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Detects electrolyte disturbances, thyroid dysfunction that can mimic or worsen ASD symptoms.
Identifies chromosomal abnormalities associated with ASD.
Excludes HIV‑related neurodevelopmental delay, common in East Africa.

b: Severe self‑injurious behaviour.
New onset seizures.
Marked regression of language after a period of stability.
sections.p: Complications arise from associated intellectual disability, epilepsy, and behavioural problems.

b: Behavioural: Applied Behaviour Analysis (ABA), speech and occupational therapy – first‑line.
Education: inclusive classrooms with visual supports.
Medication: low‑dose atypical antipsychotics (e.g., risperidone) for severe irritability; avoid sedatives that worsen cognition.
sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: early behavioural therapy, educational support, and treatment of comorbidities. Pharmacology is reserved for specific symptoms.

b: Quarterly developmental assessments until school age.
Screen for epilepsy, sleep disorders, and anxiety each visit.
Promote prenatal nutrition, malaria prophylaxis, and HIV prevention.
sections.p: Regular review of developmental milestones, school performance, and emerging comorbidities. Primary prevention focuses on maternal health and early detection.

b: Intellectual disability – global cognitive delay without the characteristic restricted interests.
Global developmental delay – non‑specific delay without the ASD behavioural pattern.
Childhood‑onset schizophrenia – hallucinations/delusions present, not typical in ASD.
sections.p: Conditions sharing social‑communication deficits or repetitive behaviours can be mistaken for ASD.

b: Normal EEG does not rule out epilepsy that may emerge later.
Absence of a known genetic mutation does not exclude ASD.
sections.p: Normal basic labs do not exclude ASD; genetic testing may be unavailable, leading to under‑recognition of syndromic causes.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of previously acquired language.
